articles.title: The Guards on St. Isaac's Square
articles.dek: During the siege of Leningrad, a band of starving scientists guarded a priceless seed collection with their lives. Peter tells scattered believers that God guards their inheritance, and that he guards them as well.
articles.quote: The same God who keeps your inheritance is keeping you, every step of the road between here and there.
articles.body:
In the winter of 1941, the city of Leningrad was sealed shut. German and Finnish forces had closed the ring around it in September, and by late November the daily bread ration for many residents had fallen to 125 grams, a slice about the size of a palm, much of it padded with cellulose. People burned their furniture and their books to stay warm, and they boiled leather belts and wallpaper paste to make something like soup. Thousands died every day, in the streets and in cold apartments, and the great city went quiet under the snow.

On St. Isaac's Square stood a building that held one of the largest stores of food left in Leningrad, and almost nobody touched it. Inside the Institute of Plant Industry lay a collection gathered over decades by the botanist Nikolai Vavilov and his colleagues: hundreds of thousands of samples of seeds, grains, nuts and tubers from five continents. It was a library of the world's crops, built so that if disease or disaster ever wiped out a harvest, humanity would have a way to begin again. The scientists who stayed behind packed the seeds into boxes, carried them to the basement, took turns guarding them from rats and from desperate people, and kept the rooms just warm enough to stop the samples from freezing.

They were starving too. Dmitri Ivanov, a specialist in rice, died in January 1942 surrounded by thousands of packets of rice he had refused to eat, and by most accounts several of his colleagues died in the same way before the siege lifted in 1944. When spring came, the survivors planted the potato collection in a field near the front so the living tubers would stay viable, working under the threat of shelling. The collection came through the war intact. Seeds from it, and the crops later bred from them, have gone into fields around the world ever since, so the bread and rice on many tables today owe something to people who held grain in their hands and kept it for strangers.

Their story is a picture of an inheritance guarded at enormous cost, and it opens a window onto the first lines of Peter's first letter. Peter wrote, most likely from Rome in the early 60s AD, to Christians spread across five Roman provinces in Asia Minor, the land we now call Turkey. He greets them as "God's elect, exiles scattered throughout the provinces" (1 Peter 1:1). The Greek word for exiles, parepidēmoi, describes resident foreigners, people who live in a place without fully belonging to it. Most of these believers had never moved house. They had become strangers in their own hometowns the moment they followed Jesus, losing standing with neighbors and sometimes with family, and living under the kind of quiet slander that wears a person down (1 Peter 2:12).

Picture this letter being read aloud in a crowded room in Cappadocia. One listener has been cut out of the family business, and another has stopped being greeted in the marketplace. The letter comes from Peter, the fisherman who once swore beside a charcoal fire that he had never known Jesus (Luke 22:54–62), and who was later met by the risen Lord on a beach and given his calling back (John 21:15–19). A man with that history knows what a second beginning feels like, and so he opens with praise:

"Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! In his great mercy he has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that can never perish, spoil or fade. This inheritance is kept in heaven for you, who through faith are shielded by God's power until the coming of the salvation that is ready to be revealed in the last time." (1 Peter 1:3–5)

The word inheritance, klēronomia, reaches deep into Israel's story. Israel's inheritance was the land of Canaan, and the Old Testament is honest about how fragile that gift proved to be in human hands. Armies overran it again and again, and at last its people were carried off to Babylon (2 Kings 25:21). Against that history Peter describes an inheritance with three Greek words that all begin with the same sound: aphthartos, which cannot decay; amiantos, which cannot be stained; and amarantos, which cannot fade. The last word is related to the amaranth, a flower the ancients prized because it seemed never to wilt.

The Leningrad scientists gave everything they had to protect the seeds, and in the end there was no one strong enough to protect the guardians. Peter's sentence holds a quieter wonder. He uses two different guarding words, one for the treasure and one for the people. In verse 4 the inheritance is "kept," tetērēmenēn, a perfect-tense form describing something placed under watch and still safely there. In verse 5 the believers themselves are "shielded," phrouroumenous, a military word for a garrison stationed around a town, and its present tense pictures a guard that never goes off duty. Paul uses the same verb when he promises that the peace of God "will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7). One way to read Peter's words is as a double watch: God guards the inheritance waiting at the destination, and he posts his own garrison around the travelers on the road toward it.

Peter is honest that the road is hard. In the very next breath he speaks of grief "in all kinds of trials" (1 Peter 1:6) and compares faith to gold that is "refined by fire" (1 Peter 1:7). The trials are real, and they hurt. Yet they happen inside the garrison's walls, on a road God has already promised to see his people through. Peter adds a tender line for readers who, like us, never walked beside Jesus in Galilee: "Though you have not seen him, you love him" (1 Peter 1:8). The love they feel is itself one of the signs that the guard is holding.

Many Filipinos know the exile's ache from the inside. Perhaps you are a nurse working night shifts in London, or a seafarer months from home, or a student in Manila who misses the province every evening. Perhaps you are the only believer at your family's table, and you have learned to stay quiet when the jokes begin. It is easy in those places to wonder whether your faith will last, as if everything depended on how tightly you could grip it. Peter says you are shielded "through faith," but the power doing the shielding is God's. Faith is the hand you lift toward him, and his hand is the one that holds.

Before you sleep tonight, you might write verse 5 on a small card or in your phone with your own name in it: "I am shielded by God's power until the coming of the salvation that is ready to be revealed." Read it on the jeepney, in the break room, or in the quiet minute before a hard conversation. When you feel worn out and far from home, let it remind you that your keeping rests on God's strength, which does not run low the way ours does.

The scientists on St. Isaac's Square kept seeds for children they would never meet, and their faithfulness still feeds the world. God has done something even more generous for you. He has prepared an inheritance that will never rot or wilt, and he has stationed himself around your life so that you will arrive to receive it. The same God who keeps your inheritance is keeping you, every step of the road between here and there.

articles.title: The Tallest Tree Stands on Borrowed Roots
articles.dek: Ezekiel's great cedar sheltered whole nations, then fell when it grew proud of its height. The tallest trees on earth hold a quieter secret about how anything great stays standing.
articles.quote: God measures a cedar by how many it shelters, and he measures us by how many can rest in our shade.
articles.body:
In 2006, two naturalists walking a remote slope of California's Redwood National Park found a coast redwood that was later measured at about 116 meters, taller than a 35-storey building. They named it Hyperion, and it is still counted among the tallest living trees on earth. You would expect a giant like that to have roots that plunge deep into the rock like the foundations of a skyscraper. It does not. A coast redwood's roots usually run only two to four meters deep, which is astonishingly shallow for a tree that size.

The secret is that the roots spread sideways, sometimes thirty meters out from the trunk, and they reach toward the roots of neighboring redwoods. They tangle, weave together, and in some cases even fuse with the roots of the trees beside them. Foresters have long observed that a redwood standing alone in a cleared field is far more likely to be thrown down by a storm than one standing in a grove. The tallest trees in the world stay upright largely because they are holding on to one another underground, where no one sees it.

I thought of Hyperion while reading one of the strangest and most beautiful chapters in Ezekiel, a poem about a tree so tall that it forgot it needed anyone at all.

The date matters. Ezekiel 31:1 places this word "in the eleventh year, in the third month on the first day," which scholars place around June of 587 BC. Ezekiel was living among the exiles in Babylon, and back home Jerusalem was under siege by Nebuchadnezzar's armies. Many in Judah were pinning their last hopes on Egypt, the old superpower to the south, to march north and rescue them. Just before this chapter, God had already told Ezekiel that he had "broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt" (Ezekiel 30:21). Egypt would not be the savior anyone hoped for.

So God gives Ezekiel a message for Pharaoh, and it begins with a question: "Who can be compared with you in majesty?" (Ezekiel 31:2). Then, instead of answering directly, God tells a story about another empire. "Consider Assyria, once a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches overshadowing the forest; it towered on high, its top above the thick foliage" (Ezekiel 31:3). Every listener would have felt the weight of that. Assyria had been the terror of the ancient world, the empire that swallowed the northern kingdom of Israel. Yet its capital, Nineveh, had fallen in 612 BC, only about twenty-five years earlier. Pharaoh was being asked to look at the stump of the last giant.

What surprises me is how lovingly God describes that cedar before it falls. Deep springs fed it. "All the birds of the sky nested in its boughs, all the animals of the wild gave birth under its branches; all the great nations lived in its shade" (Ezekiel 31:6). Even the trees in the garden of God could not match it. And then comes a line I had read past many times: "I made it beautiful with abundant branches, the envy of all the trees of Eden in the garden of God" (Ezekiel 31:9). God himself takes credit for the tree's greatness. Its height was a gift, and for a long season that gift was spent on shelter. Birds raised their young in it, and the animals gave birth beneath its branches.

Then the poem turns.

"Because the great cedar towered over the thick foliage, and because it was proud of its height, I gave it into the hands of the ruler of the nations." (Ezekiel 31:10–11)

The Hebrew phrase behind "proud of its height" is literally "its heart was lifted up in its height" (wayyarom levavo). The verb rum means to rise or be high, the same word used for the tree towering upward. Ezekiel is playing on it. The trunk rose, and then the heart rose with it, and those are two very different kinds of growth. One way to read this is that the cedar's sin was a change of attention. It stopped looking down at the creatures in its shade and started looking sideways at how far above the other trees it stood.

The consequence in verse 12 is heartbreaking in its quietness: "All the nations of the earth came out from under its shade and left it." Everyone who had once lived under its branches simply walked away. A tree that thinks it stands alone eventually does stand alone, and that is exactly when the storm finds it. The rest of the poem follows the cedar down into the realm of the dead, where it lies among others who were once mighty, and God closes the lesson to Pharaoh with a sobering line: "Which of the trees of Eden can be compared with you in splendor and majesty? Yet you, too, will be brought down" (Ezekiel 31:18).

This chapter is about empires, but it reads like a parable for anyone God has made tall. Most of us are a cedar to someone. You may be the eldest child who became the family's provider, the ate or kuya whose salary pays for a younger sibling's tuition. You may be a supervisor whose team waits on your mood each morning, a parent whose children grow up in your shade, or a church leader people call when trouble comes. That height is a gift from God, and it is good. Ezekiel never criticizes the cedar for being tall. The trouble begins when the heart starts keeping score of the height and forgets the nests.

The signs are usually small. A provider begins to remind the family, a little too often, who pays for everything. A manager stops asking the newest employee for an opinion because, after all, who knows more? A respected parent can no longer say "I was wrong" to a grown child. None of these feel like pride from the inside. They feel like being tired of carrying everyone. But slowly the birds stop nesting, and the people who once rested in our shade begin, very politely, to come out from under it.

The beautiful thing is that Scripture does not leave the image of the sheltering tree on the ground. Centuries later, Jesus described the kingdom of God as a tiny mustard seed that grows into a tree, "so that the birds come and perch in its branches" (Matthew 13:32). The birds return, but this time to a tree whose greatness began in smallness and never forgot it. And Jesus himself, who was higher than every cedar, knelt to wash his disciples' feet. In God's economy, height exists for the sake of shade. God measures a cedar by how many it shelters, and he measures us by how many can rest in our shade.

That is where the redwoods help me. The tallest trees on earth have shallow roots on purpose, and they survive because they reach out and hold on to their neighbors. Humility, seen this way, is the root system that lets a tall life stay standing. It is the willingness to admit that you need the people beneath and beside you as much as they need you. The pastor needs a friend who can correct him. The provider needs a sibling who can say "thank you, and also, please rest." The boss needs the young employee who sees what she missed.

Today, think of one person who lives in your shade, and do something that is purely for their shelter, with no reminder of what it costs you. Then think of one person whose roots you need, and tell them so, plainly and gratefully. A cedar that keeps its eyes on the nests and its roots tangled with its neighbors can weather a great deal, and God delights to make such trees beautiful.

articles.title: The Pilgrim Songs Begin With a Sigh
articles.dek: The fifteen songs Israel sang on the road to Jerusalem start far from the city, with one tired person admitting they cannot stay where they are. That honest groan is the first step home.
articles.quote: Holy dissatisfaction is often the first gift God gives to someone he is about to lead home.
articles.body:
In December 2009, Domino's Pizza did something few large companies would ever risk. It aired its own customers' complaints on national television. In grainy focus-group footage, ordinary people said the crust tasted like cardboard and the sauce tasted like ketchup. Patrick Doyle, then head of the company's American business and soon to become its chief executive, looked into the camera and admitted that the criticism had hit home. The company's chefs threw out the old recipe and rebuilt the crust, the sauce, and the cheese from the beginning. Within months sales had climbed sharply, and the campaign became a case study taught in business schools as one of the boldest turnarounds in the food industry.

What stays with me about that story is where the comeback began. Before there was a better pizza, someone had to sit in a room, hear the words "this is not good," and agree with them. The new recipe was the second step. The first step was an honest, uncomfortable admission that things could not go on as they were.

The Bible has a song that begins exactly there. Psalms 120 to 134 carry a small title in Hebrew, shir hamma'alot, which means "a song of ascents" or "a song of going up." Most scholars believe these fifteen short psalms were sung by Israelite pilgrims as they traveled to Jerusalem for the great festivals. Jerusalem sits high in the Judean hills, so from almost anywhere in the land the road climbs, and the pilgrims sang as they walked. Families from distant villages would gather, load their donkeys, and set out together, and these songs kept their feet moving and their hearts pointed toward God's house.

You would expect the first song on such a journey to describe the destination. Instead, Psalm 120 opens far away from Jerusalem, in a place of trouble. "I call on the LORD in my distress, and he answers me," the singer begins (Psalm 120:1). Then the trouble comes into view: "Save me, LORD, from lying lips and from deceitful tongues" (Psalm 120:2). This person is living among people whose words cannot be trusted, people who twist, flatter, and slander. The singer asks what will become of such a tongue, and answers that God will deal with it, "with a warrior's sharp arrows, with burning coals of the broom bush" (Psalm 120:4). The broom bush was a desert shrub whose roots made charcoal that burned hot and long, the same plant Elijah sat under when he was too exhausted to go on (1 Kings 19:4). Lies, the psalm suggests, have a way of setting things on fire, and God will answer fire with fire.

Then the singer names where they live, and the names are strange. Meshek was a people of the far north, listed among the descendants of Japheth (Genesis 10:2) and usually placed in the rugged country of what is now Turkey. Kedar was a nomadic tribe of the Arabian desert, descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:13), living in black goat-hair tents far to the south. No one could live in both places at once. The poet is using them the way we might say "I am living among strangers at the ends of the earth." The words describe a feeling of exile more than an address on a map.

"Woe to me that I dwell in Meshek, that I live among the tents of Kedar! Too long have I lived among those who hate peace. I am for peace, but when I speak, they are for war." (Psalm 120:5–7)

This is how Israel chose to begin its songs of worship on the road: with a sigh. The late pastor Eugene Peterson, in his well-loved book on these psalms, observed that the journey toward God usually starts with exactly this kind of dissatisfaction, a clear sense that where we are is wrong. The pilgrim cannot get up and walk toward Jerusalem until they have admitted that Meshek is no place to stay. Their "woe to me" is the first footstep.

Two small details in the Hebrew deepen this. The word for "distress" in verse 1 is tsarah, which comes from a root meaning narrow or tight. It describes the feeling of being hemmed in, with walls closing around you. A few psalms earlier the same idea appears with its happy ending: "When hard pressed, I cried to the LORD; he brought me into a spacious place" (Psalm 118:5). The second detail is the verb tense. Many scholars point out that verse 1 can be read in the past: "I called to the LORD in my distress, and he answered me." One way to read the psalm, then, is as a testimony sung by someone who already knows how the story turned out. Before describing the narrow place, the singer tells us that God heard. The memory of an answered prayer gives them the courage to name the present pain honestly.

The last word of Psalm 120 in Hebrew is "war." Yet only two songs later, the pilgrims are standing inside the city gates, singing, "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem" (Psalm 122:6), and the word shalom, peace, rings through the psalm again and again. The road that begins among people who love war ends in a city where peace is prayed over every wall. The singer who said "I am for peace" in a hostile land finally arrives where peace is at home.

Many Filipinos know Meshek and Kedar from the inside. It may be a crowded dormitory abroad where the gossip never stops, an office where people smile to your face and speak against you in the group chat, or a family where every attempt at reconciliation is met with an old grudge. You have tried to keep the peace, and when you speak, they are for war. Out of good manners or a wish to stay strong, many of us learn to pretend it is fine. Psalm 120 gives a believer permission to stop pretending and to say plainly to God, "Too long have I lived here."

The psalm also shows what to do with that honesty. The singer never answers lies with lies, and they leave the arrows and the burning coals in God's hands. Their part is to call on the LORD, to keep being a person of peace, and to begin walking. You might take a quiet moment today to name your Meshek in a single honest sentence before God, then pray the first verse aloud as your own: "I call on the LORD in my distress, and he answers me." After that, take one small step toward the house of the Lord, whether that means returning to a church gathering you have drifted from, calling a trusted friend who prays, or simply opening the next psalm and reading on.

Domino's could not bake a better pizza until it admitted the old one was not good enough. In a far deeper way, God often lets us feel the ache of the narrow place so that we will finally get up and go toward him. Holy dissatisfaction is often the first gift God gives to someone he is about to lead home. If you are tired of where you are living today, in your heart or in your circumstances, that weariness may be the opening line of your own song of ascents. The road climbs, and he walks it with you, and the city at the top is full of peace.

articles.title: The Kiss of an Honest Answer
articles.dek: In a book full of warnings about flattery, Proverbs compares a straight answer to a kiss on the lips. The image is stranger, and more tender, than it first appears.
articles.quote: Because God told us the truth about ourselves and then carried it, we are free to tell the truth to one another with tenderness.
articles.body:
In May 2005, at the Rome Masters, Andy Roddick stood one point away from victory. He was then one of the best tennis players in the world, facing a young Spaniard named Fernando Verdasco, and on match point Verdasco's second serve was called out. The double fault should have ended the match. Roddick had every right under the rules to shake hands and walk off the court a winner.

Instead, he walked over to the spot on the red clay where the ball had landed, looked at the mark, and told the chair umpire that the serve had been good. The call was reversed, play went on, and Verdasco came back to win the match. People who follow tennis still bring up that moment, sometimes more readily than the trophies Roddick lifted, because on clay the truth leaves a mark in the dirt and he chose to point to it when silence would have paid him well.

Few of us will ever play a match point in Rome, yet we face small versions of Roddick's choice all the time. A friend asks what we really think of a plan we suspect will hurt them, or a supervisor asks who made the costly mistake, and in that moment we can let a convenient verdict stand or walk over to the mark and say what is true. A short paragraph near the end of Proverbs 24 speaks directly into that moment, and it closes with one of the most surprising images in the whole book.

The paragraph begins with a phrase that sounds almost like an afterthought: "These also are sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 24:23). Just before it comes a longer collection, Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22, which the NIV titles the "Thirty Sayings of the Wise." These four verses are a small appendix, like a teacher who has finished the lesson and then says, before the students leave, that there is one more thing they need to hear. What the teacher adds is about courtrooms, and about the mouth.

In ancient Israel, justice was usually done in the open, at the city gate, where the elders of the town sat to hear disputes (Ruth 4:1–2). There were no anonymous judges in faraway buildings. The man deciding your case probably knew your father, owed money to your neighbor, or hoped to marry his son into the richer family standing across from you. Into that crowded, familiar setting, the sage speaks a plain warning: "To show partiality in judging is not good" (Proverbs 24:23).

The Hebrew phrase behind "show partiality" is hakker panim, which means, quite literally, "to recognize faces." A partial judge looks at the face before he looks at the facts. He sees who is standing in front of him, remembers what that person can do for him or against him, and lets that memory decide the case. Moses had given the same command to Israel's first judges: "Do not show partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike. Do not be afraid of anyone, for judgment belongs to God" (Deuteronomy 1:17).

Filipinos know this temptation by name. We call it palakasan, the system in which the person with connections gets the permit, the promotion, or the lighter sentence. Everyone has heard someone at a checkpoint or an office counter ask, "Kilala mo ba ako?" (Do you know who I am?), which is precisely the question the partial judge is always asking in his heart. Proverbs says that whoever bends the truth for the familiar face "will be cursed by peoples and denounced by nations," while "it will go well with those who convict the guilty, and rich blessing will come on them" (Proverbs 24:24–25). Then, right after those weighty courtroom words, the writer reaches for the most personal picture he can find.

"An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips." (Proverbs 24:26)

The Hebrew is compact and lovely. It reads something like "He kisses the lips, the one who returns straight words." The word translated "honest" is nekochim, which describes something straight, level, and right in front of you, a road with no hidden turns. An honest answer, in this picture, is speech that goes straight to the other person without detours around their feelings or around your own advantage.

The kiss matters because of what a kiss meant in that world. In the Old Testament, a kiss was a sign of loyalty, reunion, and covenant friendship. When Esau ran to meet his estranged brother Jacob, he "threw his arms around his neck and kissed him" (Genesis 33:4), and when David and Jonathan parted, they kissed each other and wept (1 Samuel 20:41). To say that an honest answer is like a kiss is to say that truth, rightly given, belongs in the same family as embrace and faithfulness. It is one of the ways love shows itself.

Proverbs also knows that kisses can be counterfeit. "Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses" (Proverbs 27:6). The most famous false kiss in history came in a garden at night, when Jesus said to the disciple who had come with soldiers, "Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?" (Luke 22:48). Flattery looks like affection and can still be a betrayal, because it leaves a person walking cheerfully toward harm. The honest answer may sting for a moment, and Proverbs still calls it the real kiss, the one given by someone who is on your side.

There is a deeper layer here that only comes into view in light of the gospel, the good news about Jesus. Proverbs 24:24 condemns anyone who says to the guilty, "You are innocent," and Proverbs 17:15 says the Lord detests the acquitting of the guilty. Yet the New Testament describes God as the one "who justifies the ungodly" (Romans 4:5). At first glance this looks like the very partiality Proverbs forbids, as though God simply looked at our faces and waved us through.

The cross is how God avoids that charge. Paul explains that God put forward Jesus as a sacrifice "so as to be just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus" (Romans 3:26). God gave the most honest answer ever spoken about human sin: he named it fully and refused to pretend it was small. Then, in Christ, he bore the sentence himself. Our acquittal is real because the verdict was carried out on someone who loved us. In that sense, the gospel is the truest honest answer and the deepest kiss at the same time.

This changes how we handle honesty in ordinary life. People who are secure in God's grace have less need to be flattered and less fear of being found out, so they can receive hard truth without collapsing and offer it without cruelty. Paul's phrase for this is "speaking the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15). Because God told us the truth about ourselves and then carried it, we are free to tell the truth to one another with tenderness.

For many Filipinos, this will feel costly, since our culture prizes pakikisama, getting along, and we often say "okay lang" when things are far from okay. Smooth relationships are a real good, and Proverbs does not ask us to become harsh. It asks us to stop treating silence and soft untruths as kindness when they are really self-protection. The loving friend chooses the moment carefully, speaks privately, and keeps the other person's good in view, and then says the true thing.

Today, you might think of one conversation where you have let a convenient verdict stand: a family member drifting into a bad decision, a coworker whose error you have been covering, or a friend who keeps asking your opinion and keeps getting a polite non-answer. Pray for gentleness, choose a quiet moment, and give them a straight word with your affection plainly visible. And when someone gives you an honest answer you did not want to hear, try thanking them, because Scripture says they have just kissed you on the lips.

Andy Roddick lost a match in Rome by pointing to a mark in the clay, and gained something that has outlasted the scoreline. Every time you walk over to the mark in love, you reflect the God who looked honestly at your life, did not pretend, and came close enough to carry the truth for you.
